---
name: own-your-diff
description: "Before any push or PR: explain the unpushed change in an HTML walkthrough, then quiz the author until they show they own the design. The pre-push hook blocks commits without a passed quiz. Use when pushing, opening a PR, or when a push was blocked by own-your-diff."

# Own your diff

The author pushes only work they can explain. You write a walkthrough, the author reads it, an examiner quizzes them, and a pass unlocks the push. The quiz checks that the author can reason about the change at the right **altitude**. It is not a memory test of the walkthrough.

Tools are in `scripts/`. Run each with no arguments for its commands.

- `quizgate` is the gate. The pre-push hook calls `quizgate check`. `quizgate install` opts a repo in. Commit the `.own-your-diff` file it writes, and the plugin's session hook installs the git hook in every clone that has it.
- `snippet` renders real git content as editor-style HTML blocks.
- `plainlint` checks the walkthrough for leftover placeholders, and notes long sentences, long paragraphs, and words to replace.
- `quizlint` checks a quiz file against [`references/quiz-file.md`](references/quiz-file.md).
- `quizstats` counts questions and pass rates by category and kind across quiz files.

## Steps

Asked for the quiz plan only, as an eval does? Do steps 1 and 2, skip the walkthrough, and write the plan of step 4 for a human examinee to the path you were given. Stop when `quizlint --plan` passes on it. Ask nothing.

### 1. Scope

Run `quizgate pending`. That is the scope: the commits a push would send that have no passed quiz. Diff them with `git diff $(quizgate base) HEAD`. Read the commit messages, and the task that produced the change if this session or its transcript has it.

Done when you can name the **target** of the task: the one thing the work set out to change.

### 2. Pick the altitude

The target sets the altitude. A change can carry both kinds.

- **Design altitude.** The default. The change introduces or reshapes an abstraction, a module boundary, a data shape, a protocol, a dependency, or how components talk. Cover the problem it solves, the shape chosen, how it fits the existing architecture, the alternatives and why they lost, the costs it adds, and what it makes easy or hard next.
- **Mechanism altitude.** The target is one mechanism, for example LLM prompt-cache hits, retry and backoff, stream backpressure, or a bug's root cause. Go through that mechanism's ins and outs: inputs, state, invariants, what invalidates or breaks it, the root cause, why the fix works, and how it was measured. Stay above function names and signatures.
- **Incidental.** Helpers, renames, plumbing, version bumps, and test scaffolding that serve the target. Give each one line and no question.
- **Trivial.** The whole change is a typo, formatting, a version bump, or a one-line config change. Write a short walkthrough. The quiz usually has no questions.
- **Docs.** The change only documents or explains behavior the code already has. Treat it as trivial: the author owned that design when it was built. A doc that sets a new rule, contract, or policy, such as a rule in AGENTS.md, makes that rule the target, at design altitude. Steps a contributor runs, such as a check to run or a version to bump, stay incidental even when a doc states them as rules.

Done when every hunk in the diff belongs to the target or to the incidental list.

### 3. Write the walkthrough

Copy `assets/explainer.html` to `$(quizgate dir)/<branch>-<short-sha>.html`. Write it as a short course: each lesson builds on the one before, and each one teaches a single idea. Fill in the template's lessons in order. Delete a lesson that has nothing to say, and renumber the rest.

Write for a reader who is new to this part of the code. Follow [`references/plain-english.md`](references/plain-english.md). Read it before you write. In short:

- Say it in everyday words first. Go technical only when the reader needs the detail to follow the next step, change the code, or answer the quiz.
- No AI fluff. Every sentence states a fact about this change. Cut throat-clearing, recaps, hype, hedges, and "not just X, but Y".
- Write simple technical English, in the spirit of ASD-STE100 and Orwell's rules. One idea per sentence, 20 words or fewer, active voice, present tense.
- Open each lesson with one sentence that says what it teaches.
- Use the short, common word, and one word for one thing on the whole page.
- Introduce one new term at a time, and define it in a plain sentence the first time it appears. Show the concrete case first, then name it, then give the rule.
- Go from the top down: the system, then the part the change touches, then the code. Each lesson stays at one level. Never use a lower-level detail before the reader has the level above it.
- Draw one diagram per level. The first shows the whole system with 3 to 7 boxes. Each diagram after it opens one box of the one before, and its caption says which box.
- Cut every word that does no work.

- Put code on the page only through `snippet` directives, each on its own line. Then run `snippet expand <file>`. Expanding again refreshes every block from git.
  - `<!-- snippet tree -->` shows the changed files.
  - `<!-- snippet diff PATH [HUNK...] -->` shows a diff, all hunks or the 1-based hunks named.
  - `<!-- snippet file PATH START END [REV] -->` shows file lines in an editor block.
- Show diffs where the target lives, and only the hunks that carry it. Use `file` blocks for code the reader needs whole, such as a new type or the core function. Incidental files appear only in the tree and in the "Also in this change" list.
- Draw each diagram as an inline SVG with the template's `new`, `box`, `arrow`, and `lbl` classes. A diagram shows the real components, with plain nouns on boxes and plain verbs on arrows, and marks what is new.
- Keep the quiz off the page.

Run `plainlint <file>`. It fails on a template placeholder left on the page. It also prints a note for each long sentence, long paragraph, hard word, and AI-fluff phrase from the lists in `references/plain-english.md`. Reread each note, and fix the prose unless the longer form is clearer. Then reread the page once as the reader, with the checklist at the end of `references/plain-english.md`.

Open the file with `quizgate open <file>` and give the author its path.

Done when the page renders with every directive expanded, `plainlint` passes and you reread its notes, and the author confirms they read it.

### 4. Quiz

Pick the examinee:

- **Human** whenever a human is in the session to answer. This is the default.
- **Agent** only on an unattended run: a headless session, an autonomous or autopilot playbook, or the human said they are away. Follow [`references/agent-mode.md`](references/agent-mode.md) instead of the rest of this step. A slow human, or a human who declines the quiz, is not an unattended run.

List every point at the target's altitude that the author must own to stand behind the push, from the whole diff, before you write a question. A point you meet late in the diff can still be the most important one. Rate each point's relevance:

- **`core`.** What the change is for, and the boundary or contract it sets. An author who misses it cannot defend the push.
- **`important`.** How the parts hold together: a failure mode, an invariant, where the next requirement goes.
- **`useful`.** A detail worth knowing that the push does not stand on.

Write one question per `core` and `important` point, 10 at most. Ask about a `useful` point only when the quiz would otherwise have no question. Stop when the points run out. A small fix usually carries one or two, a trivial change none, and incidental items none.

Ask outside in. Open with the `core` points, starting from what the change is for and its main boundary, then move inward to the mechanisms and details. Order the quiz by relevance, most relevant first. Only the closing question may follow a less relevant one.

For each question, list the key points a correct answer must cover. Every key point sits at the target's altitude. At design altitude, a point about one tool's setup step, a flag, or a config value is a mechanism detail, so it stays out of the rubric. Keep the rubric to yourself until the quiz ends.

Write the questions and options in the same plain English as the walkthrough, with the words the walkthrough used.

Ask **transfer** questions. A transfer question makes the author apply the design to a case the walkthrough did not spell out:

- Design. `rationale`: "Why this abstraction over <the rejected alternative>?" `failure`: "What breaks if <assumption> stops holding?" `extension`: "A new <requirement> arrives. Where does it go, and what changes?" `boundary`: "What does this boundary protect the rest of the system from?"
- Mechanism. `flow`: "Walk a request through <mechanism>. Where can it miss or fail?" `invalidation`: "What invalidates <cache or state>?" `measurement`: "Why did <the number> move, and what would move it back?" `failure` fits here too.

Give each question the one category it tests. Spread a quiz across categories rather than asking the same kind of question twice.

Mix three kinds:

- **Single-select.** One correct option among 2 to 4. Lead the quiz with these. They frame a point quickly.
- **Multi-select.** 3 or 4 options, any subset of them correct, for "which of these hold or break" cases. It passes only on the exact set.
- **Free-form.** The author answers in their own words. Use it where the reasoning is the point.

End the quiz with a multi-select or a free-form question that applies several points to one new case. That is where the pieces come together. Every wrong option is a plausible misreading of the change, never filler. Put options in random order and mark none of them.

Write the questions as a plan to `$(quizgate dir)/<branch>-<short-sha>.quiz.json`, in the shape of [`references/quiz-file.md`](references/quiz-file.md). Run `quizlint --plan` on it and fix what it reports before the first question.

Ask one question at a time and wait for the answer. Use the harness's structured-question tool when it has one: `AskUserQuestion` in Claude Code, `AskUser` in Droid, `request_user_input` in Codex where it is enabled. Where the tool has no multi-select, or there is no tool, ask in chat with lettered options and say whether to pick one or several. Never answer for the author.

After each select question, say which options were right and why in one or two sentences, so a wrong pick turns into a gotcha the author remembers. Grade each answer against its key points:

- **Pass.** It covers the core point with sound reasoning, or picks the right options. Wording and depth beyond the point do not matter.
- **Vague.** Ask one follow-up probe on the missing point.
- **Wrong or still vague.** Explain the gap in two or three sentences. Then ask a new question that targets the same point from another angle.

A probe or retry stays at the altitude of the question it follows. It tests the same key point in a new case, never a finer detail of how that point is implemented. At design altitude, "the gate keys on diff content, not commits" is the point. How a partial squash hashes is a mechanism detail, so it is out of bounds.

Done when every question is passed, or a point fails three times. With no questions, done when the author confirms they read the walkthrough. On three failures, stop and record nothing. Tell the author which part to reread or go through with you. If the walkthrough was the problem, say the change may be too large or unclear, and suggest splitting it.

### 5. Record

As the quiz runs, add each answer to its question in the quiz file as an attempt: the author's words or picks verbatim, your verdict, and what you told them. On a full pass, set `outcome` to `passed` and run `quizlint` on the file until it passes. Then run `quizgate record --by human`, or `--by agent` after agent mode.

Done when `quizgate pending` prints nothing. Push only if you were asked to push.

## Rules

- A pass belongs to the examinee who earned it in this session. Run `quizgate record` only after that pass.
- Push with the hook active. `--no-verify` is the human's call, never yours.
- A blocked push routes back to step 1 for the commits the hook names. The ledger keys passes on `git patch-id`, so rewording, rebasing, or squashing quizzed commits needs no new quiz. New content does.
- For a PR, draw the body from the walkthrough's Why, Scope, and Tradeoffs. The walkthrough and quiz file stay out of the tree.

# The quiz file

One JSON file per quiz, `$(quizgate dir)/<branch>-<short-sha>.quiz.json`. You write it as a **plan** before the first question, and you add each attempt and the outcome as the quiz runs. `scripts/quizlint --plan FILE` checks a plan. `scripts/quizlint FILE` checks a finished quiz. Evals and stats read this file, and a UI can render it, so keep to this shape.

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "branch": "feat/opt-in-marker",
  "base": "42c2cb8",
  "head": "0389727",
  "target": "Repos opt into the gate with a tracked marker instead of core.hooksPath.",
  "altitude": "design",
  "incidental": ["usage text of quizgate"],
  "examinee": "human",
  "questions": [
    {
      "id": "q1",
      "kind": "single",
      "category": "rationale",
      "relevance": "core",
      "prompt": "Why does the hook run quizgate from ~/.local/bin and not from the plugin's install directory?",
      "options": [
        { "label": "The install directory holds the version and moves on update", "correct": true },
        { "label": "Git refuses hooks outside the repo", "correct": false },
        { "label": "The plugin directory is read-only", "correct": false }
      ],
      "key_points": ["the cache path changes on every update"],
      "attempts": [
        { "answer": ["The install directory holds the version and moves on update"], "verdict": "pass" }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "outcome": "passed"
}
```

- **Top level.** `target` is the one thing the change set out to do. `altitude` is `design`, `mechanism`, or `trivial`. `incidental` lists what gets no question. `examinee` is `human` or `agent`. `questions` holds 0 to 10 questions. `outcome` is `passed` or `failed`, and a plan has none. Agent mode adds `findings`, one object per finding with its round, evidence, and fix.
- **Question.** `relevance` is `core`, `important`, or `useful`, and the questions run from most to least relevant, except the last. `kind` is `single`, `multi`, or `free`. A `single` question has 2 to 4 options with exactly one correct. A `multi` question has 3 or 4 options with at least one correct. A `free` question has no options. `key_points` is the rubric. `attempts` stays empty in a plan.
- **Category.** Each question has one. Design questions are `rationale` (why this over the alternative), `failure` (what breaks when an assumption stops holding), `extension` (where a new requirement goes), or `boundary` (what a boundary protects). Mechanism questions are `flow` (walk the mechanism, where it can fail), `invalidation` (what invalidates the state), `measurement` (why the number moved), or `failure`.
- **Attempt.** One per answer, in order. A probe or a retry adds an attempt with its own `prompt`, and `kind` and `options` when they differ from the question's. `answer` is the author's words verbatim, or the list of labels they picked. `verdict` is `pass`, `vague`, or `wrong`. `feedback` is what you told them. Agent mode adds `round`.

# AGENTS.md

This repo builds a small agent harness on top of an agent SDK.

## pstack is required

Every agent working in this repo works under [pstack](https://github.com/cursor/plugins/tree/main/pstack) (poteto-stack). This is not optional.

- Run every non-trivial task under `poteto-mode`. Most pstack skills are user-invoked only (`disable-model-invocation`), so you will not find them in your skill list. If the user did not type `/poteto-mode`, read `.agents/skills/poteto-mode/SKILL.md` in full yourself, including its Principles index and Harness section, before any work. Do the same for any other pstack skill a step routes to.
- Follow the playbook it picks. Copy the playbook steps into your task list and do not skip steps.
- Trivial tasks (a typo, a one-line config change) still follow the `principle-*` skills. Read the leaf principle whenever you apply it.
- Delegate through the `poteto-agent` subagent, never a generic one. In Claude Code it is in `.claude/agents/`. Elsewhere, follow the `poteto-agent` mapping in the Harness section of `poteto-mode`.
- Before you call work done, prove it against the real artifact (`principle-prove-it-works`).
- Model choices per role come from `~/.agents/pstack-models.md`. Run `/setup-pstack` to write it.

## Own your diff

The human author pushes only what they can explain. Before every push or PR, run the `own-your-diff` skill. That includes the push in pstack's Opening a PR playbook. It writes an HTML walkthrough of the change and quizzes the author on it. On unattended runs, fresh subagents quiz the authoring agent instead. The pre-push hook blocks commits that have no passed quiz. Run `.agents/skills/own-your-diff/scripts/quizgate install` once per clone to turn the hook on.

- A blocked push routes back to `own-your-diff`. Pushing with `--no-verify`, and recording a pass nobody earned, are the human's calls, never an agent's.

## Other skills

These skills add to pstack. They do not replace it.

| Need | Skill |
|---|---|
| Writing, changing, or reviewing a test | `test-audit`. Every new or changed test must pass its authoring gate. |
| Stress-testing a plan or design | `grilling`, or `grill-with-docs` to record ADRs and a glossary as you go |
| Domain terms and decisions | `domain-modeling` |
| Module and interface design | `codebase-design` |
| Editing AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, or a skill | `writing-for-agents` |
| Handing work to a new session | `handoff` |

## Layout

- `.agents/skills/` holds every skill. `.claude/skills` is a symlink to it.
- Vendored skills are pinned in `.agents/skills.lock`. Do not edit them in place. Re-sync with `scripts/vendor-skills.sh`, or `--update` to move the pins. Licenses are in `third_party/`.
- `test-audit` is an adapted port, not a verbatim copy. Edit it directly. `.agents/skills/test-audit/PORT.md` records what changed from upstream.
- `own-your-diff` is our own skill. Edit it directly. Run `.agents/skills/own-your-diff/scripts/selftest` after changing its scripts.

**Target:** The commit adds `check(run)`, a judging layer over the run log: it separates engine bugs from model mistakes by classifying judgments into invariants (engine properties, pass/fail, never skip) and behaviors (bets on the model, judged per-expectation with skip rules, measured as rates), plus cost (reported, never judged). So the target is: "check(run) judges a run by separating engine invariants from model behaviors, so one engine bug is distinguishable from one model mistake."

The target statement should be one sentence like the example: "Repos opt into the gate with a tracked marker instead of core.hooksPath."

Target: "check(run) judges a run on engine invariants (pass/fail, never skip) and model behaviors (rates that count only trials with a chance), with cost reported but never judged."

**Altitude:** This is design altitude: the change introduces an abstraction (a judging layer with a boundary: invariant vs behavior vs cost; a skip taxonomy; reads only the run log). Actually the change reshapes how a run is judged — an abstraction and a module boundary. It's design altitude. Though there are mechanism-ish aspects (why invariants read the transcript and events together — that's mechanism-flavored, but it's part of the design rationale of the boundary). The skill says "A change can carry both kinds." But the plan file has a single `altitude` field. The primary altitude here is design: the change introduces the check abstraction and its boundary. The mechanism details (e.g., a schema-rejected core__call_tool leaves no tool event) are key points but at the design level they're about the data-shape decisions (invariants read transcript+events together).

Let me think again: the target is the judging layer with its invariant/behavior/cost taxonomy. This is design altitude: it sets a module boundary (check reads only the run log; pure function over RunLog), a data shape (Report with invariants map, behaviors list, cost), a contract (invariants never skip; behaviors skip when precondition never happened; rates count only trials with a chance).

**Incidental items:**
- `RequestCost`/`Cost` reporting shape? Hmm, cost is part of the report but "reported and never judged" — is cost part of the target or incidental? The commit message says "cost is reported and never judged". Cost reporting is part of the design (it's part of the Report contract). But it's arguably a smaller part. The live test already measured usage; checks.ts re-implements requestUsage as costOf. That's a move of existing measurement into the report. I'd say cost is part of the target but a secondary aspect; the quiz can have a question about it being reported and never judged (boundary).
- The `pick` helper in tests, `strings` traversal, `ratio` rounding — mechanism details, incidental.
- The test scaffolding (faux scripts, broken runs standing for engine bugs) — that's actually part of the design: "Both tables are typed by the check names, so a check added without its cases does not compile". That's a design point about how the tests enforce the table. Is that target or incidental? The commit message devotes a paragraph to it: "Its tests type both case tables by the check names, so a check added without a passing and a failing case does not compile, and each failing case asserts the evidence that names its mistake." This is a real design choice about the test structure. It's `important` maybe, not core. Hmm. The skill says test scaffolding that serves the target is incidental ("Give each one line and no question"). But this is not mere scaffolding — it's a compile-time guarantee that every check has cases. I'd rate it `important` or `useful`. Let me think about points below.

Now, per the skill: "List every point at the target's altitude that the author must own to stand behind the push, from the whole diff, before you write a question. Rate each point's relevance: core / important / useful."

Let me enumerate points at design altitude:

1. **The separation itself: invariants vs behaviors.** Why: the live test asserted three ad hoc properties and logged the rest, so an engine bug and a model mistake looked alike. The check layer separates them: an invariant is an engine property every trial must keep (one failure = a bug in the engine); a behavior is a bet on the model, measured as rates across trials (a failure is a data point about the model, not a bug). Core. Category: rationale ("Why two classes instead of one list of assertions?") or boundary. I'd ask: "Why split the checks into invariants and behaviors instead of one list of pass/fail assertions?" Key points: engine vs model responsibility; a failing invariant names an engine bug; a failing behavior is a model data point (rate over trials, not a bug); that's why rates exist — one trial failing a behavior says nothing about the engine.

2. **The skip rule and its asymmetry.** Invariants never skip (nothing to wait for; a run with nothing to check passes); behaviors skip when the precondition never happened (use without the model enabling the plugin; skill whose plugin never enabled; any behavior on a step the run never reached) so rates count only trials that had the chance. This is core — it's the boundary/contract of the behavior rate. Category: could be `boundary` (what the skip protects rates from) or rationale. A good transfer question: "A run's report shows use@1 as skip. What does that mean for the rate?" Or a failure question: "What goes wrong with the rate if a behavior counted a no-chance trial as a fail?" Key points: a skip is excluded from the rate (not counted as fail); precondition examples (model never enabled plugin → use skips; plugin never enabled → skill skips; step never ran → all behaviors on it skip); invariants can't skip because there's nothing to wait for.

3. **The boundary: check reads only the run log.** check(run) is a pure function over RunLog (public types only), so the live test, `aigent check` CLI, and the future multeval grader get the same verdict from the same files. Core — this is the boundary the change sets. Category: boundary. "What does 'check reads only the run log' buy?" Key points: one verdict from the same files for every caller (live test, CLI, grader); the run log/result directory is the whole input; enables re-grading old runs; the check can't depend on in-memory state of a live session.

4. **Why invariants read the transcript and the events together.** Because no listener sees creation-time records (you can't subscribe before the session is returned), and a schema-rejected core__call_tool leaves no tool event, only an error result in the transcript under the same call id. So the RunView merges both sources: enabled-at-start comes from transcript slice (0..start), dispatch-recover finds rejections only in the transcript. This is core/important — it's a data-shape decision. Category: rationale or failure. I'd rate it core or important. It's the reason the judging layer is built over RunLog which carries both. Key points: events alone miss creation-time records (subscribe happens after creation, so records written at creation reach no listener; enabledAtStart is recovered from transcript entries before log.start); transcript alone misses nothing? Actually events carry tool_end outcomes and turn structure (turn_end closes the enabling turn for `use`). And schema-rejected calls leave an error toolResult in the transcript but no tool_start event, so dispatch-recover must read the transcript to find them. So both sources are needed for different facts.

Hmm, wait — is this design altitude or mechanism? The commit message explains it as part of the design (why the checks read both). I'd list it as core (it's in the commit message as a key paragraph) or important. Let me rate: core. Actually, let me think about what's "core": "What the change is for, and the boundary or contract it sets." The transcript+events decision is how the data shape supports the checks — it's a contract of the run log (why RunLog carries both steps[].events and transcript, and the start marker). I'd say important-leaning-core. The quiz can have at most... one question per core and important point, 10 at most. Let me enumerate more.

5. **Each behavior owns its precondition/skip rule** (as opposed to a shared skip logic). "Behaviors. Each owns its precondition, so its skip rule." This is a design point about where the skip logic lives. Maybe fold into point 2.

6. **Cost is reported and never judged.** Cost (tokens, cache ratios) appears in the Report but no check passes or fails on it; it's measurement, not verdict. Core or important? The commit message headline includes it: "cost is reported and never judged." Why: cost varies by model/provider/infra, not by correctness; judging it would make a cheap wrong answer look better. It's a boundary point: the report separates verdicts from measurements. I'd rate important (the push doesn't stand on it as much as the invariant/behavior split, but it's a contract). Could be a multi-select option or part of a question.

7. **The invariants table as the list; types derive from it.** The `invariants` table is keyed by name; `Invariant` type and the Report's invariants keys derive from the table, so an invariant added without an implementation doesn't compile (similar for judge's `satisfies never`). Similarly the test case tables are typed by check names so a check added without passing and failing cases doesn't compile. This is the "make the table the source of truth" design pattern. Important. Category: rationale or failure. Key points: the table is the single list; types derive from it (Report keys, Invariant union); tests can't miss a check (compile-time exhaustiveness via satisfies); each failing case asserts evidence naming the mistake, so a check that fails for the wrong reason is caught.

8. **The invariant list itself (the five invariants and what each protects):** secret-free (scrub worked; no raw secret in the log, detected via the LEAKED mark), enabled-before-call (no tool runs before its plugin's enabled record, per session), resume-keeps-plugins (saved prefix unchanged + no re-enable), denial-recorded (every denied outcome has a matching denied record), enable-text-once (pending text delivered exactly once, in the first user message after it). At design altitude, the specific list is what the boundary protects the rest of the system from... Hmm. The five invariants are engine properties the checks assert. Knowing all five by heart is more mechanism/detail? No — these are the contracts. But quizzing "name all five invariants" is a memory test. Better: ask about one or two at design level, e.g., why secret-free detects the mark rather than the raw value (because the scrub already replaced raw values with [LEAKED:NAME] marks; the check reads the run log which is already scrubbed, so it looks for marks). Hmm, that's mechanism. At design level: the invariant checks the run log holds no raw secret — but the run log is produced by the scrub, so the check validates the scrub, and leaksIn finds marks. A question could be: "secret-free passes on a scrubbed log. What does it actually look for, and why does that catch a leak?" That's mechanism altitude-ish. The skill says to stay at the target's altitude. For design altitude, the key point is: invariants are engine properties; one is enough to name a bug. Maybe a question on what a failing invariant means for the push (engine bug vs model mistake) — that's point 1.

Let me also think about the behaviors list: discover, restraint, use, dispatch-recover, follow, skill, denial, host-enable, resume — nine behaviors. Their preconditions: discover skips if already enabled before the prompt; restraint never skips (always judged); use skips if the model didn't enable the plugin in the prompt (or plugin enabled before? use requires cause === 'model' within the prompt); dispatch-recover skips in native mode and when no core__call_tool was rejected; skill skips when plugin never enabled; denial skips when no matching call was denied; host-enable/resume are judged on any ran call (preconditions are enforced by the scenario parser at authoring time: host-enable requires an enable step since the previous prompt, resume requires a resume step — the parser enforces these, so the checks don't need to skip on them). That's an interesting design point: preconditions that the scenario format can guarantee at parse time (host-enable needs an enable step; resume needs a resume step) are enforced by the parser, not by skip rules — the skip rule is only for preconditions that depend on what the model or the run did. That's a nice design point, important.

9. **Behavior id `${check}@${step}` unique per scenario** — one check per step enforced by the scenario parser (a second "discover" on one step would share its id). The id is the metric name for reports and future grades. Useful/important. The uniqueness rule is enforced at parse time ("a second X on one step would share its id"). That's a small design decision: the id is the join key for grading; parse-time rejection keeps ids unique. Useful.

10. **`use` semantics: the turn right after the model enables the plugin must call the tool.** The enabling turn is closed by the first turn_end after the enabled record; the next turn's calls are judged. This is a bet definition (the design's bet: a good model uses the tool immediately after enabling it). Mechanism-ish detail of one behavior. At design altitude, each behavior's definition is a bet the design makes. Probably important-to-useful. Could be a question: "use@1 fails when the model enables weather in turn 1 and calls get_weather in turn 3. Is that a bug or a data point, and what does the check bet on?" Hmm, that mixes point 1 with a mechanism. The skill says one question per point, and the points should be at target altitude.

11. **dispatch-recover's design**: in dispatch mode, a core__call_tool rejected before it runs has no tool_start, only an error toolResult in the transcript; the behavior judges whether the model recovers by calling the real tool next turn. Skips in native mode (native declares the tool, so no core__call_tool exists to be rejected). Also requires the plugin already enabled, to rule out "enable its plugin first" as the rejection. That's a subtle design choice. Important.

12. **Invariant tests can't be made to fail by a model script** ("No script can make a correct engine break an invariant, so an invariant's broken run is a correct run with one fault, named for the engine bug it stands for") — the test strategy: behavior failures are scripted model mistakes; invariant failures are correct runs with one injected fault (mutating the log). And each failing case asserts the evidence that names its mistake, so the check fails for the right reason. Important. Category: rationale (why fault injection instead of a broken engine).

13. **The `entriesOf` strict parser: any unknown role or malformed known one throws** ("a check over a misread transcript would be wrong without saying so"). Design decision: fail loudly on transcript shapes it doesn't know, rather than silently ignoring. Important. Category: failure ("What happens when the transcript contains a message shape entriesOf doesn't know?") — it throws; the alternative (ignore) would silently produce wrong verdicts.

14. **`recordOf` trusts the brands** ("The brands mean 'in the catalog', which the engine checked when it wrote the record") — the check re-validates record shape but trusts plugin names because the engine validated them at write time. That's a contract with the engine: checks don't re-run the catalog. Useful/mechanism.

15. **The report's `complete` field**: false when a prompt ended error/aborted or a step threw (log.steps shorter than scenario.steps). Useful. Part of the Report shape.

16. **Cost details**: promptTokens = input + cacheRead + cacheWrite; cachedRatio per request and overall; steps per prompt; turns from RunResult. Mechanism details. Incidental at design altitude.

17. **The scrub/leaksIn contract**: secret-free finds [LEAKED:name] marks; the scrub guarantees raw values never appear (longest first replacement, keys included). The invariant validates the scrub end-to-end. The check looks for marks, not raw values, because by the time check sees the log, raw values are already replaced — a mark is the witness of a leak. Important-ish. Category: measurement? No, that's mechanism category. At design altitude: the boundary "the run log is scrubbed; checks read the scrubbed log; secret-free is the engine's guarantee restated as an invariant." Could fold into a question about invariants.

Now the quiz: one question per core and important point, 10 at most. Order: core first, from "what the change is for" inward. End with a multi-select or free-form applying several points to one new case. Spread categories: rationale, failure, extension, boundary (design altitude categories).

Maybe: "Why can a behavior skip but an invariant cannot?" Key points: a behavior has a precondition (a chance to show); counting a no-chance trial as fail would poison the rate (blame the model for something it never had the opportunity to do); an invariant has nothing to wait for — the engine either kept it or broke it in what ran; a run with nothing to check passes vacuously (evidence counts: calls, resumes, denials show the pass is not vacuous — that's the exercised evidence in tests).
- C3. The boundary: check reads only the run log; same verdict from the same files for live test, CLI, grader. → q3, category boundary: "What does judging only from the run log buy the design?" Key points: every caller gets the same verdict from the same files; result directories can be re-graded offline (multeval grader); the check needs no live session, no model, no engine; the run log's shape (transcript + events + saved transcripts + start marker) is exactly what the checks need.

Key points: creation-time records reach no listener (subscribe can only happen after the session is returned), so enabled-at-start must be read from the transcript before log.start; a schema-rejected core__call_tool produces no tool event, only an error toolResult in the transcript (dispatch-recover finds it there); events carry what the transcript lacks: tool outcomes (tool_end with outcome denied/ran), turn boundaries (turn_end closes the enabling turn for use). So the run log must carry both, and the view merges them per step.

Important:
- I1. Cost is reported, never judged. → maybe fold into a multi-select question with the skip rule? Or a single: "A run costs 10x more than another. What does the report say about it, and why is that all?" Key points: cost lands in the report as numbers (tokens, cached ratios), no verdict keys on it; cheap-vs-expensive is not correctness; cost explains variance in results, not pass/fail. Category: boundary.

Tables derive types: the invariants table is the list (Invariant and Report keys derive from it); the judge switch is exhaustive; the test case tables are keyed by check names, so a check without pass+fail cases doesn't compile. → category failure or extension: "A dev adds an `efficiency` behavior tomorrow. What stops it from shipping unjudged or untested?" Key points: judge's default `e satisfies never` fails to compile without a case; behaviorCases typed `satisfies { [K in Expectation['check']]: BehaviorCase }` requires a case; the scenario parser's expectations table and FIELDS also need an entry (check names flow through parse→judge→test). Extension category fits.
- I3. Test strategy: no model script can break an invariant on a correct engine, so invariant failures are injected faults on correct runs; each failing case asserts the evidence naming the mistake. → category rationale: "Why do the invariant tests mutate a correct run instead of scripting a bad model?" Key points: an invariant is an engine property — the faux model can't break it; a scripted "bad" run would test the fixture, not the engine; a fault stands for a named engine bug; asserting evidence guards against a check that fails for the wrong reason.
- I4. dispatch-recover: why it exists, its skips (native mode; no rejected core__call_tool; plugin not yet enabled → the rejection doesn't count), and why it requires the plugin already enabled. → Hmm. This is one behavior's detail. At design altitude, the interesting point is: recovery is judged from evidence that exists only in the transcript (error result, no tool_start), and the "plugin already enabled" condition rules out enable-first as the rejection. I could fold the transcript evidence into C4 (which already covers the schema-rejected core__call_tool). Then dispatch-recover's skip rules (native mode skip) could be an option in the skip question. I think one question on dispatch-recover specifically might be too mechanism-y. Let me fold it: C4 covers the transcript+events merge with dispatch-recover as the concrete case.
- I5. Preconditions enforced at parse time vs at check time: host-enable needs an enable step since the previous prompt, resume needs a resume step — the scenario parser rejects a scenario that lacks them (before any paid run), so those behaviors never need a skip for them; skip rules are only for preconditions that depend on what the run did. → category boundary/extension. This is a real design point: where a requirement is checked (authoring time vs run time). Key points: parse-time validation costs nothing and refuses before a paid run; skip-time handles what the model does (which can't be known up front). Could be a good single-select: "host-enable has no skip rule for 'the host never enabled the plugin'. Why not?" Because the scenario format guarantees it: an enable step since the previous prompt, or parseScenario rejects; whereas 'the model never enabled the plugin' (use) can't be guaranteed up front, hence skip.
- I6. Behavior ids: `${check}@${step}`, unique per scenario (one check per step enforced at parse), the metric name a report and future grade use. → useful.
